claims.claim: Pharmacokinetics is the study of what the body does to a drug over time; the term combines pharmaco (medicines) and kinetics (movement), and OpenStax's Pharmacology for Nurses defines it as how the body processes the medicine.
The four primary processes of pharmacokinetics are absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (the ADME shorthand used by the NLM's MeSH vocabulary).
Absorption is the movement of a drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream, and the route of administration influences how quickly and completely a drug is absorbed.

Drugs enter the body by several routes — by mouth (oral), directly into a vein (IV), through the skin (topical), and by inhalation — and IV drugs enter the bloodstream immediately with no absorption barrier.
Distribution is the movement of a drug through the blood to the body's tissues; the blood and lymphatic systems are the primary transport vehicles, and drugs do not spread evenly to all tissues.
Barriers can limit distribution: the blood–brain barrier is a protective system that keeps many drugs from entering the central nervous system.
Metabolism (biotransformation) is the chemical alteration of a drug by the body; the liver is the primary site, where enzymes change drugs into forms that can be more readily eliminated.

For oral drugs, medication absorbed from the intestine passes through the liver before reaching the general circulation (the first-pass effect), which can reduce how much active drug reaches the body.

Excretion is the removal of drugs from the body; most drugs, particularly water-soluble drugs and their metabolites, are eliminated by the kidneys through urine, with other routes including bile/feces, the lungs, and the skin.
Kidney function affects drug elimination: renal disorders can increase a drug's action and duration because the drug is not cleared as quickly, and providers may adjust dosing.
Half-life is the time it takes for a drug's blood concentration to fall by 50 percent, and it helps determine how often a drug is given.
Pharmacodynamics — what the drug does to the body — is a distinct concept from pharmacokinetics, which is what the body does to the drug.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Naming the phases and the final phase's label: OpenStax and MeSH name the four processes absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, while Merck Manual's consumer section titles its pages 'Drug Absorption,' 'Drug Distribution Within the Body,' 'Drug Metabolism,' and 'Drug Elimination' and describes elimination as removal of drugs (metabolized or intact) from the body.
positions: OpenStax Pharmacology for Nurses: 'The four primary processes of pharmacokinetics are absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion.'
NLM MeSH: ADME and ADMET are abbreviations for absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination (and toxicology).
Merck Manual (Consumer): 'Drug elimination is the removal of drugs from the body... Most drugs... are eliminated by the kidneys through urine.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the four-phase names absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (OpenStax, MeSH), notes the kidneys as the main exit route, and attributes the removal statement to both OpenStax and Merck — the sources agree on the underlying science and on the kidneys being the primary route.

sourceRecords.title: Pharmacology for Nurses (OpenStax), Section 2.2 Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry id reused with the identical canonical URL. Read live 2026-08-22; the pharmacokinetics content was read at the book's section 2.2 page (https://openstax.org/books/pharmacology/pages/2-2-pharmacokinetics-and-pharmacodynamics). Supports: pharmacokinetics as how the body processes the medicine (pharmaco = medicines, kinetics = movement); the four primary processes of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion; absorption definitions and routes (skin/topical, respiratory tract/inhalers, GI tract/oral, subcutaneous/IM) with IV entering the bloodstream immediately and being 100% bioavailable; distribution through the blood and lymphatic systems with uneven spread and the blood–brain barrier as a protective barrier; metabolism as chemically changing a drug into a form more readily eliminated, occurring primarily in the liver, with the first-pass effect for oral drugs; excretion primarily through the renal system via urine with other routes (lungs, skin, bile, feces); kidney disease increasing a drug's action and duration; half-life as the time for serum concentration to fall by 50%. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Drug Absorption (Merck Manual Consumer Version)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (full review Aug 2026, author Jennifer Le, PharmD). Supports: drug absorption as the movement of a drug into the bloodstream after administration; absorption affecting bioavailability — how quickly and how much of a drug reaches its site of action; factors including the drug product's design, the drug's physical and chemical properties, and the person's physiology. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Drug Distribution Within the Body (Merck Manual Consumer Version)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (full review Aug 2026, author Jennifer Le, PharmD). Supports: drug distribution as the movement of a drug to and from the blood and various tissues of the body and the relative proportions of drug in those tissues; once absorbed, most drugs do not spread evenly throughout the body. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Drug Metabolism (Merck Manual Consumer Version)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (full review Aug 2026, author Jennifer Le, PharmD). Supports: drug metabolism as the chemical alteration of a drug by the body; most drugs must pass through the liver, which is the primary site for drug metabolism, where enzymes (a specific group of cytochrome P-450 enzymes) convert drugs to active or inactive forms. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Drug Elimination (Merck Manual Consumer Version)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (full review Aug 2026, author Jennifer Le, PharmD). Supports: drug elimination as the removal of drugs from the body; all drugs are eventually eliminated, either after being metabolized or intact; most drugs, particularly water-soluble drugs and their metabolites, are eliminated by the kidneys through urine, so drug dosing depends largely on kidney function; other routes include excretion in bile. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
